content: Sweating sickness, also referred to as the English sweat (Latin: sudor anglicus), was a mysterious and highly virulent disease that emerged in England and later spread to parts of Europe in a series of epidemics. The first outbreak occurred in 1485, and the last was recorded in 1551, after which the disease seemingly disappeared. The onset of symptoms was abrupt and dramatic, often leading to death within hours. The exact cause of the disease remains unknown. It is important to note that hyperhidrosis, a separate medical condition characterized by excessive sweating, is sometimes informally referred to as sweating disease, but it is unrelated to the historical sweating sickness. The disease first gained the attention of physicians at the start of Henry VII's reign. It was noted shortly after Henry's landing at Milford Haven on August 7, 1485, and was being discussed even before the Battle of Bosworth Field on August 22. By the time Henry arrived in London on August 28, the disease had broken out in the capital, killing several thousand people by late October of that year. Among the victims were two lord mayors, six aldermen, and three sheriffs. This alarming illness, soon known as sweating sickness, was recognized as distinct from the plague and other known epidemics due to its unique symptoms and rapid, often fatal progression. After the initial outbreak in 1485, the disease reappeared in 1507, though this second epidemic was less severe. A third outbreak occurred in 1517, which was far more devastating. In towns such as Oxford and Cambridge, the disease was frequently fatal, with reports suggesting that up to half the population in some areas perished. This outbreak also spread to Calais and Antwerp but did not extend beyond England, with these exceptions. The fourth outbreak in 1528 was particularly severe. It began in London at the end of May and quickly spread across England, though it did not reach the far north, Scotland, or Ireland. Mortality in London was significant, prompting the court to disperse, and Henry VIII frequently changed his residence to avoid the disease. Anne Boleyn is believed to have contracted and survived the illness. Remarkably, this epidemic spread across Europe, appearing suddenly in Hamburg and causing over a thousand deaths within weeks. The disease then spread rapidly through Eastern Europe, reaching Switzerland in December, and subsequently moving north to Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, and east to Lithuania, Poland, and Russia. It did not, however, appear in France or Italy. In Belgium and the Netherlands, the disease likely spread directly from England, as it appeared simultaneously in Antwerp and Amsterdam on September 27. In each location, the disease typically lasted no more than two weeks before disappearing. By the end of the year, it had vanished from most areas, lingering only in eastern Switzerland into the following year. After this, the disease did not reappear on mainland Europe. The final major outbreak occurred in England in 1551. John Caius, a prominent physician, provided an eyewitness account of the disease in his work A Boke or Counseill Against the Disease Commonly Called the Sweate, or Sweatyng Sicknesse. According to Caius and other observers, the disease began suddenly with a sense of apprehension, followed by cold shivers (sometimes severe), dizziness, headache, and intense pain in the neck, shoulders, and limbs, accompanied by profound exhaustion. The cold stage, lasting from 30 minutes to three hours, was followed by a hot and sweating stage. The characteristic sweat appeared suddenly without an obvious cause. This was accompanied by a sensation of heat, headache, delirium, rapid pulse, and intense thirst. Palpitations and chest pain were common. No skin eruptions were observed. In the final stages, patients either succumbed to general exhaustion and collapse or experienced an overwhelming tendency to sleep, which was thought to be fatal if indulged. Surviving one attack did not confer immunity, and some individuals suffered multiple episodes before succumbing. The disease was never seen again in England after 1578, although a similar illness, known as the Picardy sweat, occurred in France between 1718 and 1861. The Picardy sweat was less fatal and was accompanied by a rash, which was not a feature of the earlier outbreaks. The cause of sweating sickness remains one of its most enigmatic aspects. Contemporary and modern commentators have speculated that the unsanitary conditions of the time, including widespread dirt and inadequate sewage systems, may have harbored the source of infection. The first outbreak coincided with the end of the Wars of the Roses, leading to speculation that French mercenaries brought the disease to England. These mercenaries, employed by Henry VII, appeared to be immune to the illness. Interestingly, the disease seemed to affect the wealthy more severely than the poor, which may explain why it was considered noteworthy compared to other illnesses of the time. Relapsing fever, a disease spread by ticks and lice, has been proposed as a possible cause. This illness typically occurs during the summer months, as did sweating sickness. However, relapsing fever is characterized by a prominent black scab at the site of the tick bite and a subsequent skin rash, neither of which were noted by contemporaries of sweating sickness. More recently, hantavirus has been suggested as a potential cause. While hantavirus presents an intriguing possibility, certain clinical features of hantavirus outbreaks do not align with the progression of sweating sickness. For example, hantavirus is rarely transmitted from person to person, whereas human-to-human transmission was believed to be a significant mode of spread for sweating sickness. Although hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) shares a similar clinical picture with descriptions of sweating sickness, unanswered questions leave room for alternative theories regarding its etiology.
